analysis.one_liner: Lets workers sue employers in court — with real damages — for firing or penalizing them over union activity.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in two House committees from July 2014 until the Congress ended in January 2015, backed by 18 Democrats and no Republicans.
analysis.plain_summary: Under federal labor law, if an employer fires or punishes a worker for supporting a union, the worker's only real option is to file a charge with the National Labor Relations Board, which can order back pay but cannot award damages for emotional distress, punish the employer, or make the employer cover legal bills. This bill would have given workers a second option: sue the employer in federal court, like workers can already do for race or sex discrimination, and win compensatory and punitive damages plus attorney's fees. The bill was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced, then to a Judiciary subcommittee in September 2014, and no committee ever acted on it. It died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who are fired, demoted, or otherwise penalized for supporting a union — or refused a job because of union sympathies — would gain the right to sue in federal court and win compensatory and punitive damages and attorney's fees, remedies the National Labor Relations Board cannot order. Workers considering organizing would gain leverage, because retaliation would carry a real price tag instead of at most back pay. Labor unions benefit indirectly from stronger organizing conditions.

how_it_helps.text: Under current law, a worker fired for union activity can only ask the National Labor Relations Board for a remedy, and the Board cannot award compensatory or punitive damages or order the employer to cover the worker's legal fees. This bill lets the worker instead sue in federal court and win back pay, compensatory and punitive damages, and court-ordered relief.

The bill lets a court award attorney's fees — including expert witness fees — to the prevailing party, modeled on the remedies available in employment discrimination cases, so a fired worker could hire a lawyer without paying up front.

It covers employer discrimination in hiring, tenure, or any term or condition of employment aimed at encouraging or discouraging union membership — the core retaliation and anti-union discrimination provisions of the National Labor Relations Act.
The bill gives workers 180 days from the violation to file suit, keeping the window comparable to existing federal employment claims.

analysis.who_pays: Employers would bear the cost: exposure to federal lawsuits, jury-awarded compensatory and punitive damages, and prevailing-party attorney's fees for labor-law retaliation claims, on top of the existing National Labor Relations Board process. Businesses would also face added litigation costs, and some cases could proceed in court even while a Board charge was pending.

drawbacks.text: The bill would add a second track of litigation on top of the National Labor Relations Board process: an employee could file with the Board and also sue in federal court, and courts could award compensatory and punitive damages under the civil-rights statutes it borrows from, exposing employers — including small businesses — to jury trials and larger awards than the Board can order.

The 180-day filing deadline and the courtroom route shift enforcement from a specialized labor agency with labor-law expertise to generalist federal courts, which critics of similar proposals say can mean slower resolution and less consistent labor-law rulings.

Because attorney's fees go to whichever party prevails, an employee who brings a losing suit could be ordered to pay the employer's legal fees, a risk that could deter some low-wage workers from filing at all.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the benefits are substantial: real money damages and a lawyer's fees would give the NLRA's anti-retaliation protection actual teeth for the first time. The honest costs run to employers, who would face a parallel track of federal lawsuits — including suits seeking punitive damages — on top of NLRB proceedings, and smaller businesses with the least legal capacity would feel that most. Some of the delay and backlog critics point to is real, but the fee-shifting provision was written to screen out weak suits: a worker who loses in court can be ordered to pay the employer's fees. The bill died in committee without any recorded objection, so no one had to defend or defeat it on the merits.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees when introduced in July 2014, was sent to a Judiciary subcommittee in September, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Keith Ellison introduced the bill on July 30, 2014, and the Speaker referred it to two committees: Education and the Workforce, and Judiciary.
Eighteen House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.
On September 26, 2014, the Judiciary Committee referred it to its Subcommittee on the Constitution and Civil Justice, where bills commonly go to wait.
Neither committee ever held a hearing, marked the bill up, or reported it out, and no version of it was ever debated or voted on in the House or Senate before the Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers are better off: firing or retaliating against workers for union activity still carries no risk of compensatory or punitive damages or fee awards. Committee leaders also avoided a recorded vote on a labor measure.

for.name: Rep. Keith Ellison
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Employee Empowerment Act to give workers a private right of action under the National Labor Relations Act.

for.role: Cosponsors, including John Lewis, John Conyers, George Miller, and Raul Grijalva

sides.party_line_note: All 19 supporters were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; with Republicans holding 232 of 435 House seats and controlling the committee schedule, the bill never reached a vote.

industries.note: Today, firing or discriminating against a worker for union activity carries little financial risk beyond Board-ordered back pay. The bill would let workers sue for compensatory and punitive damages plus attorney's fees, the same exposure employers face in discrimination cases.

The bill strengthens enforcement of the rules protecting workers who organize, and union organizing drives are far more viable when firing organizers carries real damages. Unions' interest here runs alongside the workers' interest.
A new private right of action with fee-shifting creates a market for lawyers to take retaliation cases on contingency, which is also what makes the remedy accessible to low-wage workers.
